On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya is the armed prince who orders Sitaram to open the door, draws his sword on him, and then disarms and binds Sitaram with his own cloth, leaving him tied up on the ground. On the night of Udayaditya's own escape, the dynamic reverses: Sitaram enters Udayaditya's prison, orders him to come out because of the fire, grabs and nearly carries him out, and leads him, while Udayaditya—now the passive prisoner—asks helplessly what to do and where to go.

Pratapaditya's initial failed plan was to have two Pathan men kill Basanta Ray when he sheltered at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore; the Pathan refused to carry out the murder and confessed instead. The method that finally succeeded was Pratapaditya's signed death sentence for the King of Raigarh, carried out when Muktiyar Khan summoned Abdul, who entered Basanta Ray's prayer room with a drawn sword and killed him (beheading), after which Abdul emerged with a bloodied sword and a stream of blood flowed in the room.

In Jessore's inner quarters (zenana), disguised as a woman—a middle-aged woman in female attire with a head-cloth—Rammohan Mal seized Ramai, pulled the cloth from his head, lifted and swung him in the air, then bound him with a shawl and carried him out over his shoulder like a sack; and in the king's chamber/audience hall where Ramai sat as the jester beside the king, Rammohan Mal grabbed him by the scruff of his neck and threw him out of the room.

Rukmini (Mangala) brewed a lethal poison with mantras over five days and had Matangini secretly fetch it for the Rajmahishi; Surma then took the poison—reported as suicide by her own hand—and died, which covertly removed her from the palace instead of exile to her father’s house.

The Maharaj, Ramchandra Ray, feels gravely insulted by her refusal and resolves to take another wife in revenge; consequently, when Vibha finally travels to Chandradwip, she discovers the Maharaj is getting married that very day, shattering all her hopes of reunion and happiness.

Rukmini obtains Udayaditya's signet ring from him in Chapter 21, and its seal bears the Yubaraj's name engraved on it. In Chapter 22, Sitaram and Bhagavat use that ring's seal to stamp a forged petition falsely accusing Udayaditya of treason against Pratapaditya; Bhagavat then presents this forged, sealed petition to Pratapaditya, who uses it as the pretext to order Udayaditya's imprisonment.

Ramchandra Ray’s midnight escape required Udayaditya to overpower and bind the palace guard Sitaram, who was subsequently dismissed from his job along with Bhagavat. Feeling responsible, Udayaditya began paying them monthly stipends from his own funds. When Pratapaditya learned of this, he forbade any further aid. Surma, unable to bear their hunger, secretly continued sending the stipends through a trusted maid (known only to Mangala). Upon discovering these secret stipends, Pratapaditya ordered Surma to be sent to her paternal home; when she refused, he threatened to imprison Udayaditya, compelling her exile.

The song expresses profound loneliness and bereavement: everything once “mine” has vanished, leaving only emptiness, with no one left to sing for, answer the singer’s call, or embrace, leaving him to wonder how to go on living with only himself.

He sings it first alone on his palace veranda in Raigarh at sunset, gazing at the mango grove in private melancholy while remembering those who used to listen to him and the joyful days he would travel to Jessore to see loved ones, fearing he may never see them again. He sings it a second time in Jessore, taking Vibha’s hand in the silent, dark, empty inner quarters before Surma’s deserted room, slowly singing it to her in shared sorrow after confronting the desolate reality that those who were there are no more.

Rukmini's failure allows her to reach Pratapaditya's court and reveal that Udayaditya escaped with Basanta Ray; Pratapaditya then sends Muktiyar Khan with a secret order for Basanta Ray's execution. Rukmini identifies Udayaditya in the field, leading to his capture, after which Muktiyar Khan goes to Raigarh, presents Pratapaditya's signed death warrant to Basanta Ray, and has him beheaded.

Pratapaditya initially received Ramchandra coldly and dismissively—without a proper welcome or musical fanfare, sending only the Dewanji late with a small escort, then meeting him in his chamber with no joy while attending to state business and curtly sending him to the inner quarters, thereby asserting his superiority. Later, in Ramchandra’s own court, Ramchandra reverses the slight by publicly diminishing Pratapaditya’s status: courtiers claim Pratapaditya’s family were upstarts whose first king had to beg for anointment from Ramchandra’s grandfather, Ramai Bhand mocks Pratapaditya’s lineage as earthworm and leech, and Ramchandra is immensely pleased by daily verbal attacks, joking that his marriage into Pratapaditya’s family redeemed Pratapaditya’s line and that bringing Vibha to Rajpur would lower Ramchandra’s court.

She returns as Mangala, the renamed widow Rukmini living on the outskirts of Jessore; having won over the palace servants, she prepares a poison with roots, mantras and tantric rites and supplies it to the Rajmahishi through Matangini to kill Surma so she can win Udayaditya back, causing Surma’s death, and later she enters his bedchamber by lamplight during a storm, accusing him of ruining her and demanding his love and his ring.

Udayaditya’s early lament—wishing he had never been born crown prince, calling himself unfit to rule, and describing his father’s constant testing, neglect, and rejection—culminates when, brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner, he agrees that he is unworthy of the kingdom. He formally asks to be released from the throne, requests that Samaraditya be named heir, and before Ma-Kali, with Pratapaditya as witness, swears that as long as he lives he will not accept even an iota of Jessore’s kingdom, sit on its throne, or touch its royal scepter, invoking the sin of his grand-uncle’s murder upon himself if he ever does; he then departs for Kashi.

Nayanchand, afraid to deliver the letter to Pratapaditya in Jessore, intercepts it and gives it to the Mahishi. Basanta Ray then reads it and, concealing its true contents—that Ramchandra Ray had renounced Vibha and said she must not be sent to Chandradwip—instructs the Mahishi to announce that Ramchandra had written requesting that Vibha be sent to her in-laws’ house. The Mahishi conveys this false version to Vibha and proclaims it throughout the household, leading Vibha to believe her husband had summoned her back.

Rammohan and his followers pull Ramchandra Ray’s boat up and over the large sal wood logs blocking the canal, bypassing Pratapaditya’s blockade, while the guards are too disorganized and delayed to intercept them in time; the boat then continues down the canal to the Bhairav river.

Basanta Ray leaves his sitar behind when parting from Udayaditya, declaring he will not play it anymore; later in Raigarh his “eternal companion” is no longer with him, its strings broken and “it can no longer be tuned,” while Khan Saheb notes that no one hears his singing or music anymore—so the silenced, broken sitar mirrors his loneliness and despair over Udayaditya’s absence and imprisonment.

Earlier, he would have stopped the oppressor without considering the consequences and tried to protect the subject; after Surma's death, fear of Pratapaditya makes him hesitate and refrain—he turns away and goes into his house instead of intervening.
By freeing Udayaditya from prison: during the fire, Sitaram enters his cell, tells him the prison is on fire, and grabs and carries him out of confinement.

On the first occasion (Chapter 11), to rescue Maharaj Ramchandra Ray, Rammohan twists several thick sheets into a rope, ties it to a pillar on the palace roof above the canal, straps Ramchandra to his back, climbs down the rope—gripping it with his teeth at the end—carefully lowers Ramchandra into the waiting boat in the canal some seventy cubits below, then jumps down himself. On the second occasion (Chapter 37), after Vibha faints before the king, Rammohan lifts her up, carries her out of the palace, and places the unconscious queen into a palanquin waiting by the gate before returning to the boat.

In Jessore, the Mahishi dresses Vibha lavishly as a royal princess—eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an elaborate coiffure—leaving her shy, joyful, and burdened by ornament. In Chandradwip, she comes dressed as a common woman, refusing a palanquin and saying she will go like a beggar; her veil falls, she enters the palace unnoticed like a maidservant, and is unrecognized and humiliated by the king.

In his bedchamber after Surma’s death, the window symbolizes painful absence and lingering grief: it is the spot where Surma used to sit, left empty, where Udayaditya vainly hopes to see her again beneath the same moonlight and garden breeze. In the prison cell, the window becomes a symbol of hope and freedom: through its small opening he sees the sky, birds, bamboo grove, and temple, and sitting there makes him feel naturally free despite captivity, reminding him that his cage may one day break, while moving away from it plunges him into darkness and forgetfulness of liberation.

It begins as a transactional flirtation: the penniless guard Sitaram repeatedly borrows money from the moneylender widow Rukmini (Mangala), trading teasing endearments and jokes while never repaying her, until they start meeting in secret to plot together. It turns hostile after Udayaditya’s imprisonment, when Sitaram curses Rukmini, threatens to burn her house and free the Yubaraj himself, and flees to Raigarh, prompting Rukmini to erupt in demonic rage and declare that the Yubaraj is “my Yubaraj” and that only she can help or harm him. It becomes life-threatening when Sitaram stages the prison fire and fakes Udayaditya’s death; believing Rukmini knows the truth and will expose him, he goes to her cottage to take her money, but finds her wet, disheveled, and ghostly in a single lamp’s light. She declares she has returned from Yama’s door, vows to burn him and the Yubaraj, and reaches for a curved blade to kill him, so Sitaram barely escapes and flees Jessore that night.

Sitaram first uses the guardhouse fire to draw the guards away from Udayaditya’s cell, leaving the prison door unguarded so he can lead Udayaditya out. The strategy then becomes a cover-up: Sitaram has his men set fire to Udayaditya’s now-empty cell, sabotages the firefighting effort so the blaze cannot be controlled, and plants bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword in the burning room. When the guards rush to the cell and find only collapsed ruins and charred remains, attention shifts from an escape to a supposed death, allowing Sitaram to spread the rumor that Udayaditya died in the fire while he and Udayaditya flee.

He feels no gratitude: he interprets Udayaditya’s protection as having been done chiefly for his own sister Vibha’s sake rather than to save Ramchandra’s life, and as something that was bound to happen anyway—so in court he sets it aside and joins the minister and Ramai Bhand in laughing at and ridiculing Udayaditya as Pratapaditya’s son, lacking the will to stop the mockery for fear of what others would think.

By fabricating a petition bearing the Yubaraj’s seal, in which Prince Udayaditya ostensibly complains to the Emperor of Delhi about Pratapaditya’s treason in order to seize the kingdom, and having Bhagavat deliver it to Pratapaditya as an intercepted letter bound for Delhi, the Emperor’s name is used to make it appear that the son is conspiring with the Emperor against his father.

When Surma is present, she styles Vibha’s hair according to Vibha’s own liking, offering a private comfort against the Mahishi’s imposed adornments; after Surma is gone, Vibha sits at braiding time waiting for Surma to come and braid her hair, but her hair remains unbraided, turning the grooming ritual into a poignant marker of Surma’s tragic absence.
